question.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function With an Irreducible Trinomial Quadratic Factor
question.worked_solution:
Notice that the quadratic factor in the denominator has a discriminant that is not a perfect square:

$$
D=(-4)^{2}-4(1)(-3)=28
$$

We have that $\sqrt{28}$ is not a rational number, which implies that the quadratic factor doesn't factor over the rational numbers.

So, we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\frac{2{x}^{2}-3x-9}{(x+3)({x}^{2}-4x-3)}=\frac{A}{x+3}+\frac{Bx+C}{{x}^{2}-4x-3}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x+3)({x}^{2}-4x-3),$ and we get

$$
2{x}^{2}-3x-9=A({x}^{2}-4x-3)+(Bx+C)(x+3)
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=1,B=1$ and $C=-2.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{2{x}^{2}-3x-9}{(x+3)({x}^{2}-4x-3)}=\frac{1}{x+3}+\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-4x-3}.
$$

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2{x}^{2}-3x-9}{(x+3)({x}^{2}-4x-3)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x+3}+\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-4x-3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-4x-3}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we have

$$
\int \frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|.
$$

For the second integral, we use the substitution $u={x}^{2}-4x-3.$ Then $\text{d}u=2(x-2)\,\text{d}x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-4x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{u})\frac{\text{d}u}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}-4x-3|\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2{x}^{2}-3x-9}{(x+3)({x}^{2}-4x-3)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-4x-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}-4x-3|+K.\end{aligned}
$$
